# Design Decisions — Symptom-to-Product Discovery Prototype

Redcare case study, Part 2. Candidate: Yunus Emre Fisek. This document walks through every material product decision behind `symptom-discovery-prototype.html`, organized to mirror the case's evaluation criteria (Search Domain Depth, ML Collaboration, UX Rigour, Health Context Awareness, Product Vision & Craft, AI Tool Fluency) so it doubles as interview prep, not just documentation.

---

## 1. Framing: intent routing, not "a symptom search"

The brief describes a gap — a customer who searches "I can't sleep" today just gets keyword-matched melatonin products, ranked by popularity, with no experience designed for someone arriving with a problem rather than a product in mind.

The instinct behind this prototype is that **"build a symptom search" is the wrong unit of design.** Different query types need fundamentally different treatment:

- A customer typing "ibuprofen" already knows what they want. Interrogating them with clarifying questions is friction, not help.
- A customer typing "sunburn" expresses a relatively low-ambiguity self-care need. It can receive a lightweight category route with an escape hatch.
- A customer typing "I can't sleep" or "my joints ache in the morning" is describing a *problem*, not a product — and problems can have multiple plausible causes, severities, and correct next steps.
- A customer typing "chest pain" is describing something that should never resolve to a product at all.

So instead of one classifier or one guided-question flow applied uniformly, the prototype implements **intent routing**: a deterministic cascade of five layers, cheapest and safest first, where each layer only escalates to the next when it genuinely can't resolve the query itself.

![Routing cascade decision flow](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
The interactive prototype is scoped to Germany. The `DE / CH / NL` Rx label in the conceptual diagram indicates a possible future Rx-market extension, not the prototype's current scope.

**Layer 1 — Safety / red-flag check.** Hard-coded list of high-risk phrases ("chest pain," "can't breathe," "intestinal bleeding," etc.). This layer runs first, always, and overrides everything else — including all four layers below it. It is deliberately **not probabilistic**. A false negative here isn't a bad recommendation, it's a safety failure, so it doesn't get the benefit of a model's judgment; it's a fixed list that a human (ultimately legal/clinical) reviews and versions.

**Layer 2 — Catalogue / direct match.** Known brand or ingredient names ("ibuprofen," "vitamin D") skip guidance entirely. A customer who already knows what they want shouldn't be slowed down by a flow designed for people who don't.

**Layer 3 — Low-ambiguity self-care taxonomy.** Selected needs with relatively low routing ambiguity (for example, "sunburn") route straight to a relevant category with no questions. This is not a claim that the symptom has one cause. The visible **"this isn't quite it →"** link re-routes into guided flow when the light route is wrong.

**Layer 4 — Long-form / natural-language classifier.** First-person, multi-word queries ("I can't sleep," "my joints ache in the morning") get 1–2 clarifying questions before resolving — never immediately, never to a single "best product."

**Layer 5 — Ambiguous fallback.** Short, under-specified queries ("pain," "tired," "stomach") get the same guided flow, but starting from broader initial questions since there's less signal to work with.

### The taxonomy boundary

The five prototype domains are deliberately not a pharmacy taxonomy. A production system needs governed mappings across: consumer language and need state; symptom or clinical concept; therapeutic goal and pharmacological class; active ingredient; formulation, route, and strength; audience and eligibility constraints; and finally catalogue product, PZN, or SKU. Pharmacists and clinical experts govern these mappings; product, search, and ML teams make them maintainable, retrievable, and evaluable.

**Why this order, cheapest and safest first:** each layer is only asked to do what it is actually good at. Layer 1 is an inspectable prototype gate, not a production safety solution. Layers 2–3 handle high-confidence catalogue intent or selected low-ambiguity self-care routes. Layers 4–5 are where genuine ambiguity is handled by asking rather than guessing.

### Two real failures that motivated this design

Live on the actual Shop Apotheke site (Redcare's German storefront):

- **"Herzinfarkt" (heart attack)** resolves directly to standard product results — zero safety escalation. This is exactly the Layer-1 failure mode the safety check exists to prevent.
- **"Herzschmerzen" (heart pain)** — genuinely ambiguous (cardiac, muscular, anxiety, reflux are all plausible) — resolves *confidently* to aspirin. This is arguably worse than the first failure: picking the riskiest interpretation and answering with false confidence, instead of asking one clarifying question first. It's the direct justification for Layer 3's escape hatch and Layer 4/5's insistence on questions before resolution.

### Safety layer: recall, not precision — and a real fix to an earlier gap

An earlier version of this prototype implemented Layer 1 as pure exact-phrase matching against the ten-item red-flag list — a query either contained "chest pain" verbatim or it didn't. That's a real gap, not a hypothetical one: "my chest feels really tight," "I can't catch my breath," and "pressure building in my chest" all describe exactly the kind of risk the layer exists to catch, and none of them match any exact phrase on the list. A safety layer whose own headline claim is "a false negative here is a safety failure, not a UX inconvenience" cannot be built on the one matching technique with the worst recall characteristics for open-ended phrasing.

The fix is a second, deliberately looser check that runs alongside the exact-phrase list: a **risk-area noun** (chest, breath, heart, conscious, faint, numb, bleeding, blood) co-occurring with a **risk modifier** (tight, pressure, can't, severe, sudden, crushing, one side, pass out, and similar) escalates even with zero exact-phrase overlap. This is explicitly a high-recall, lower-precision net — some queries it catches won't turn out to have needed escalation, and that's the correct trade-off for this one layer specifically. The routing-trace panel labels these separately ("Safety check — near-miss heuristic") so the distinction between "matched the curated list" and "caught by the broader net" stays visible rather than papered over.

This is not presented as solved. A keyword-cluster heuristic is lexical rather than semantic, so it has both false positives (for example, an anxious "my throat feels tight" query if the noun list is too broad) and blind spots (for example, "something feels really wrong and I feel cold and clammy"). The held-out eval confirms that the current safety approach fails its guardrail. The honest claim is only that the prototype makes the failure inspectable; `EVAL-METHODOLOGY.md` defines the clinically reviewed concept-level and release-gate work required before any production claim.

## 3. ML / modeling approach

The brief evaluates "ML Collaboration" explicitly, so this section is written the way it would be defended to an ML engineer in the room.

**Proposed approach: gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) on simple, structured behavioral features** — query length, catalogue-match score, historical reformulation rate, click entropy — not deep learning, not raw-text embeddings, at this stage. Three reasons:

1. **No query volume yet to justify it.** This is a net-new feature; there's no training signal until it ships and starts logging.
2. **The inputs are tabular, not raw text.** Once lexical rules (Layers 1–3) have stripped out the easy cases, what's left to classify is a handful of structured signals about *how* a query behaves, not the text itself — a tree model is the right tool for that shape of data.
3. **Explainability.** Tabular routing features can be inspected and audited. That does not make a tree model inherently safe: model choice never replaces golden-set evaluation, calibration, deterministic safety overrides, or clinical review.

**Where probabilistic methods do fit, deliberately scoped:**
- Embeddings/semantic matching — reserved for long-tail phrasing once the lexical rules in Layers 2–3 genuinely run out of coverage.
- LLM-assisted extraction — a last-resort layer, narrowly scoped to *mapping free text to a taxonomy node + confidence score*, never open-ended medical reasoning. Layer 1's safety check still runs independently on top of it and overrides it regardless of LLM confidence — an LLM never gets to be the safety net.

**The eval / golden-set question:** a seed offline eval has been built and run on 20 held-out, human-labeled queries; it found 50% safety recall, 0% sensitive-topic detection, and 50% category-match accuracy. It blocks any claim that the prototype is production-safe. Production evaluation needs a larger risk-weighted expert-labeled set, adversarial/paraphrase coverage, double labeling for sensitive cases, and a CI/release gate. The golden set must be independent of taxonomy construction and grow from anonymized production incidents and query samples.

**The line this is built to defend in the room:** *"I wouldn't build one classifier — I'd build a decision cascade where the cheapest, most explainable layer resolves as much as possible, and only escalate to probabilistic methods where lexical rules genuinely can't cope. Safety-critical routing never depends on the probabilistic layers."*
## 4. Market scoping: Germany, deliberately

**Stated assumption:** this prototype is scoped to the German market — Redcare's largest by revenue, and one of only three Redcare markets (with Switzerland and the Netherlands) where prescription medicines are actually sold. That makes the discovery/escalation boundary a real commercial decision, not just a UX one.

Why Germany specifically, and not just "a market":
- Largest revenue base (DACH segment, anchored by Germany).
- Rx-enabled — unlike most International-segment markets (Belgium, France, Italy), which are OTC-only.
- Every real-site finding used in this project (Herzinfarkt, Herzschmerzen) was already German-language — scoping to Germany formalizes what was already true, not a pivot.
- Germany has its own identifier system (PZN, used on every result card in the prototype) and its own advertising-law constraints (below) — both usable as concrete grounding rather than generic "trust matters" language.

**A fourth resolution path, enabled specifically by the Rx-market scope.** A generic cascade ends in three states: direct / category / safety-escalation. Germany's e-prescription infrastructure justifies a fourth: guided flow concluding **"this may need a prescription,"** routing toward Redcare's e-Rx flow rather than an OTC category. In the prototype this triggers when a query is tagged as an Rx-candidate (e.g. "I've had a cough for weeks that won't clear up") *and* the guided flow's duration answer is "more than 2 weeks" — otherwise the same query resolves to a normal OTC category. This path only makes product sense in an Rx-enabled market; in an OTC-only International-segment market this branch wouldn't exist at all.

## 5. Legal grounding: Germany's HWG (Heilmittelwerbegesetz)

The HWG regulates advertising of medicines in Germany. Two provisions are directly relevant here — cited as *worth legal review*, not as something already cleared:

**§11 — bans fear-inducing disease representations** and before/after-style imagery in consumer-facing advertising. The safety-escalation and referral screens' calm, factual, non-alarming tone isn't only a UX preference — it's aligned with a real legal constraint on how disease-related content can be shown to German consumers.

**§12, in conjunction with Annex A — restricts advertising that references certain diseases** to the general public. Verified against current legal sources (not assumed from memory) rather than guessed, since this is exactly the kind of detail worth being precise about in the room. Annex A (diseases affecting humans) lists exactly **four categories**:
1. Notifiable diseases/infections under the Infektionsschutzgesetz
2. Malignant neoplasms (cancer)
3. Addiction diseases, excluding nicotine dependence
4. Pathological complications of pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period

This is deliberately applied to the taxonomy, not left as an abstract caveat. Three concrete places it shows up in the prototype:

- **"This mole has changed shape"** (Annex A.2 — malignant neoplasms). Ambiguous, cancer-adjacent, and exactly the kind of query that could otherwise resolve to a confident OTC skin-product recommendation. The prototype routes it to a professional referral, never a product — regardless of the guided-flow answers given.
- **"I can't stop drinking"** (Annex A.3 — addiction diseases, excluding nicotine). Same treatment: guided flow always resolves to a pharmacist/addiction-service referral, never an OTC anti-anxiety-style product.
- **The real-site "testicular cancer" → etoposide finding** (see below) is a direct Annex A.2 hit layered on top of an existing Rx-only gate — a stronger example than either constraint alone, and the clearest illustration of why this Annex actually matters for taxonomy design, not just tone.

This turns "I'd want legal to confirm which terms are affected" from a hedge into a demonstrated method: two taxonomy phrases were actually audited against Annex A and routed accordingly, not just flagged as a general concern.

**A scoping caveat worth being upfront about:** §12 governs *advertising* — whether a symptom-discovery screen that never names a product for these two queries counts as "advertising referencing a disease" in the statute's sense is itself a question for legal, not something this prototype resolves by asserting it. For both "this mole has changed shape" and "I can't stop drinking," the primary, load-bearing reason for a referral-only outcome is straightforward clinical judgment — neither should resolve to a confident OTC product regardless of what any advertising statute says. HWG §12 is presented here as *additional* grounding that happens to point the same direction, not as the reason the design decision was made. Overstating a legal citation's centrality to a product decision it didn't actually drive is its own credibility risk, worth naming rather than leaving implicit.

## 6. Additional real-world evidence (from the live Shop Apotheke site)

- **"Testicular cancer" → etoposide** — correctly labelled prescription-only/doctor-administered, so the primary risk (self-selection) is already mitigated by the Rx gate. The softer, unconfirmed gap: the product description may not specifically name it as a chemotherapy agent within a defined oncology protocol, versus reading as a generic prescription drug — flagged as worth validating with the clinical team, not a confirmed failure.
- **Undifferentiated facets** — the live site's filter panel mixes human OTC/vitamin facets with veterinary facets (animal species, life stage) regardless of query context, and "Show more" reveals long undifferentiated lists. Not a routing/safety issue, but evidence that discovery-quality problems exist beyond the entry point — relevant context for the broader design rationale, less central to this prototype.

## 7. Visual and content design

- **Palette:** deep teal (trust) + brick-red (alerts, reserved *only* for the hard-stop safety screen) + sage (reassurance, used for the softer referral screen so it reads as "needs a professional," not "emergency"). The distinction between brick-red and sage is itself a design decision — conflating "call 112 now" with "please see a doctor when convenient" into the same visual urgency would undersell the former and oversell the latter.
- **Typography:** Fraunces (serif) for headlines, IBM Plex Sans/Mono for body and UI — chosen deliberately away from the generic rounded-sans-serif "AI product" look, closer to how an established pharmacy brand would actually typeset.
- **The routing-trace panel** (monospace, dark teal) is the prototype's signature UI element: after every query, it shows which of the five layers handled it and why, in plain language. This turns the cascade architecture into something demonstrable on screen during the live walkthrough, instead of something that only exists in an explanation.
- **PZN-style reference codes** (e.g. "PZN 04837261") on every result card — a small authenticity touch that signals awareness of the real German pharmaceutical identifier system without claiming real catalogue integration.
- **Design-decision callouts** embedded directly on each screen state — the same rationale text used in this document, visible in the product itself, so the live walkthrough can point at the UI rather than switch to slides.
## 8. Deployment

The prototype is a complete, self-contained app already — a single `.html` file with vanilla JS/CSS, no build step, no dependencies, no backend. Opening the file in any browser runs it. What's needed is a stable public URL for the review session.

Key features of this architecture worth being able to explain verbally:
- The **safety layer sits outside the routing service's normal decision path** — deterministic, versioned, and legal-reviewed, not something the rest of the system can accidentally route around.
- **Rx resolution only exists as a path because of the Germany/CH/NL market scope** — in an OTC-only market this branch wouldn't exist.
- The **eval pipeline validates before release**, not after — a gate, not a dashboard.
- Query logs feed golden-set growth over time — the eval isn't a one-off artifact, it's a living part of the system that connects back to §3's ML approach.

## 10. Product discovery: ranking, not just categorization

The brief and the role are both explicitly about *search* — and an earlier version of this prototype under-delivered on that specifically. The cascade decided *which* category or product set to show, but was silent on *order*: every result was an unordered list. For a Search PM, that's the wrong thing to be quiet about — deciding which items appear is only half of product discovery; deciding the order they appear in is the other half, and it's the half with the ranking, relevance, and personalization problems in it.

The prototype now labels the first card in any multi-product result **"Top match"** and the rest **"Also relevant,"** with an explicit `Ranked by: symptom-category relevance, then popularity (mock)` note above the grid. This is deliberately illustrative, not a real ranking model — there's no click data or catalogue behind this prototype to rank against. What it's meant to demonstrate is the *habit*: never present a result set without being able to say why it's ordered the way it is. In a real implementation, the ranking signal for a resolved category would likely blend:

- Category-match confidence from the cascade layer that resolved the query (a Layer-3 light-route match is higher-confidence than a Layer-5 ambiguous-fallback resolution, and that confidence should be visible to the ranker)
- Historical click-through and reformulation rate within that category — the same structured features proposed for the cascade's own classifier in §3, reused rather than duplicated
- Stock, price-tier, and any commercial placement rules, kept clearly separate from relevance so the two are never silently conflated

## 11. Commercial trade-offs

Every non-purchase outcome in this cascade — safety escalation, HWG-flagged referral, and Rx-routing — ends a search session without a sale. That's a real cost, not a hand-waved one, and the prototype now says so explicitly: each of those three screens carries a "Commercial trade-off" callout naming what's being given up and what would need to be true for the trade to be worth it (e.g., an escalation is worth its lost conversion if it protects trust; whether it actually does is an empirical question, not an assumption).

The concrete way I'd validate this in production, beyond the eval metrics in §12:
- **Return-window tracking** on referral and Rx outcomes — compare return behavior within 7–14 days with the baseline, while treating it as a behavioral signal rather than proof that a referral was clinically correct.
- **Escalation precision**, not just recall — the near-miss heuristic in §2 is deliberately tuned for high recall, which means it will over-trigger. That's the correct default for a safety layer, but "correct default" and "free" are different claims — a persistently low escalation-precision number would be a signal to invest in a smarter (still safety-first) Layer 1, not evidence the layer is broken.
- **A/B testing intent-routing against the current keyword-search baseline** before claiming this is a net-positive feature — the case brief's premise (today's melatonin-heavy results page) is a real UX gap, but "better UX" and "better business outcome" aren't automatically the same conclusion, and a Search PM's job is to hold both.

## 12. Eval & quality metrics

The prototype's header includes measured seed offline-eval results alongside explicitly TBD online metrics. It makes one structural point visible on screen rather than only in prose: **guardrail metrics and quality metrics are not the same kind of number and should not be traded off against each other.** The measured safety and sensitive-topic guardrails fail, so the prototype is not production-safe.

- **Guardrail metric — missed-escalation rate.** Target: as close to 0% as measurable. This is never traded off for a better-looking average; a system that improves overall precision by occasionally missing a genuine red-flag query has made things worse, not better, regardless of what the aggregate number says.
- **Quality metrics** — escalation precision, category-match precision by cascade layer, resolution rate, guided-flow abandonment. These behave like normal product metrics: they can trade off against each other, they're expected to move as the taxonomy and thresholds are tuned, and "worse this week, better next week" is a normal part of iterating on them.

This distinction, what a golden set actually is for this project, and worked examples of building and scoring one from this prototype's own taxonomy, are covered in full in **`EVAL-METHODOLOGY.md`** — written as a standalone reference rather than folded in here, since it's dense enough to want its own document.

## 13. Open items / honestly unresolved

- **The near-miss safety heuristic (§2) is still lexical, not semantic.** It closes the specific gap this project found (chest/breath-adjacent phrasing missing the exact-phrase list), but a fixed noun/modifier list will have its own blind spots for phrasing that doesn't use any listed word at all. It should be treated as one layer of defense that needs real query-log validation, not a solved problem.
- **Product ranking is illustrative, not real** — the "Top match" / "Also relevant" badges in §10 demonstrate that order is a decision worth making visibly, but there's no actual ranking model, click data, or catalogue behind them.
- **Safety-screen contact info** uses real, public, non-emergency-specific German numbers (116117 pharmacist/medical helpline, 112 emergency) rather than a fabricated Redcare hotline — chosen deliberately to avoid citing a fictional company contact as if it were real, while still reading as authentic rather than a bracketed placeholder.
- **HWG Annex A audit is illustrative, not exhaustive** — only 2 of the 52 taxonomy phrases were explicitly checked against it. A real taxonomy of any size would need a systematic pass, ideally with legal, before shipping.
- **The "Herzschmerzen"-style ambiguity problem is only partially solved.** The guided flow narrows by duration and one follow-up question — it doesn't yet distinguish cardiac-plausible presentations from clearly-not-cardiac ones within the "chest/heart-adjacent" bucket. A real implementation would likely want a dedicated, more conservative sub-flow for anything chest/heart-adjacent rather than folding it into the general joint/muscle bucket.
- **The seed offline eval is built and run, not productionized** — it contains 20 held-out queries and exposes failing safety and sensitive-topic guardrails. A CI/release-gate pipeline and a large expert-labeled production dataset are still to be built.
- **Query parsing / attribute extraction is not covered by this prototype.** The cascade answers "what kind of query is this" (direct / symptom / ambiguous); it doesn't extract structured attributes embedded *within* a query — form (Tabletten, Saft, Kautabletten, Tropfen...), dosage/strength, or audience (Kinder/Erwachsene). This is a genuinely separate problem from intent routing, not a missing case inside it, and it's actually the easier of the two: pharmaceutical form vocabulary is small and closed (perhaps 20-30 terms across markets), which makes it a good fit for a lightweight dictionary/gazetteer lookup rather than anything probabilistic. The right architecture is a parallel pre-processing step that enriches the query with structured filters *before* the cascade runs, so whichever layer resolves intent (direct match, light category, or guided flow) can apply the same filters — rather than re-solving form-detection separately inside each layer. Not implemented here; scoping it out was a time trade-off, not an oversight discovered late.
